review_text_raw:
I liked Mainlining at first, because I like the visual style and it also has a backstory (unlike most other "hacking" games).
I would forgive the bad UX of the command prompt and the incompleteness of the universe (e.g. websites only exist for the time of the missions in which they appear) and some other minor issues.

But the dealbreaker for me is how stupid the missions are. You have to identify perpetrators, collect evidence against them and find their whereabouts. Okay - that COULD be fun. But a huge part of the problem is that - when you get one of the ingredients wrong, you get no useful information on WHICH ingredient was wrong. If the location isn't correct, then why does the newspaper say that the suspect had been "wrongly accused" and "released"? This phrasing indicates that the location was right but the evidence to weak. Okay - so the feedback is misleading and (once you have figured THAT out!) you have to look at the clues and logically deduce the ingredients. Right? That would constitute a PUZZLE-game. That would make sense. That would be fun. But that's not how Mainlining rolls.

Oftentimes you have to submit a piece of evidence that would never hold up in court - even when you have collected much better evidence that isn't accepted. Also you often have evidence against multiple suspects. So you are already guessing between 6 to 30 combinations of these two ingredients. As to the whereabouts: you have access to everybodys addresses, but usually there is a vague hint to a different location in one of the files - and I mean VAGUE. And if there isn't such a hint, you are still always in doubt whether you have overlooked one. AND ON TOP OF THAT there are sometimes twists that require leaps in your reasoning that only make sense in hindsight. Mission 7 in particular was so harebrained that I FURIOUSLY uninstalled the game after reading that insult of a "solution" in a walkthrough.

I'm convinced that Rebelephant wasted to much time on side-gimmicks like the "maps" view, ran out of time in development and could only design a handful of missions, so they deliberately made the solutions illogical to artificially extend the playing-time. Illogical puzzle games aren't fun, they are frustrating. VERY FRUSTRATING. So although I really want to like this game - I can only advise you to STAY AWAY from it!

review_text_raw:
Well, I like the idea of the game and I found its story somewhat enjoyable. There are many nods to actual existing software. But even when I knew exactly what I had to do, I sometimes just looked into a walkthrough to spare myself from having to go through all the annoying gameplay mechanics again. Instead of repeating what other people have already said, let me first point you to two well-written negative reviews that pinpoint exactly what made the gameplay kind of a chore:

https://steamcommunity.com/id/algorithman/recommended/454950/

https://steamcommunity.com/id/Oloko0/recommended/454950/

In addition to that, the concept of the missions is sometimes weird. Every mission ends by arresting a single suspect. Sometimes you just have 1 suspect, sometimes there are 3 possible suspects and you just have to arrest any of them, not all 3. That's also the case in a mission where you're just told to find information on a person who went missing years ago. You can randomly find information on her ex-husband, arrest him for producing drugs with her, and you win. And the game just never even follows up on that, except in the credits where you suddenly find out that the missing person is dead.

There's other weird stuff going on like a puzzle in the final mission where you need to find the suspect's son's first name, and in the ending, he suddenly has a different name. I also found a placeholder document that said something like "Following the suspect's arrest on [date the player arrested him]"

Mainlining is much more of a point-and-click thriller with an annoying interface rather than a hacking game, but I did not expect a simulation anyway. You can finish it in 4 hours and I kinda enjoyed it for the most part, but it's super unpolished and vague and the devs never bothered releasing an update. I wouldn't buy it unless it's heavily discounted.

Out of all those hacking and investigation games like Hacknet, Hacker Evolution, Orwell, The Black Watchmen, and Hypnospace Outlaw, this is the one you can skip.

Look, I'm sorry. This "gripping narrative" is inferior to Hacknet/Uplink/Hypnospace Outlaw/Insert Desktop Simulator Here in every single possible way. The fact that missions are bite sized and don't really tie together terribly well doesn't help, and it's horribly obtuse in terms of "puzzles" which are best summarized as downloading everything and attempting to use brute force to incriminate the target of the mission, because the file you think would work never does.

The characters are generic and uninteresting. The setting is generic and uninteresting. The web pages are generic and uninteresting. The console is generic and uninteresting. The interactions are generic and uninteresting. I could go on. I didn't think it was possible to fail at constructing a narrative this badly and still have people eat it up and leave positively glowing reviews.

There are better games to play if it's this genre. I can't actually recommend this in good faith, since it's just...not that good. It's like a Michael Bay film, except that this version of Michael Bay makes badly animated explosions that will only keep your attention if you've never seen a better explosion.

While I enjoyed my first 3 hours of the game, I ran into a bug that first appeared to inhibit my progress in the game. While the bug seemed like a significant oversight in the development process, one bug is understandable and after doing an online search I determined that you could still complete the mission while the bug was being worked on.
What made Mainlining an utterly frustrating experience for me was receiving specific instruction in the game that were not correct. There is one mission in particular where your partner says you must provide a legal document to prove that someone had a name change. I did this and failed the mission.
On top of that (same mission), the suspect lived in one area, but had expressed that he was going to move back home with his parents in an email. When I tried arresting the subject in the area where his parents live, I failed the mission and was met with a message that said attempting to make an arrest in that area failed to produce a suspect. I then tried to make an arrest where the suspect stated he lived. I was met with another message that I failed the mission, but that the area I made the arrest produced the suspect. I thought to myself, okay, I now know this person lives in this area, but I must have the wrong evidence. This was a little frustrating already given that my AI partner said I had to provide legal evidence of a name change and that's the evidence I was presenting.
I then tried evidence after evidence, clicking through documents and trying them out in my arrest attempt with the same suspect in the area where he said he lived. I kept receiving fail messages. I thought, okay, maybe I completely missed a small detail and have the wrong suspect.
I reviewed each document in the mission and determined that either I'm totally missing something or I'm experiencing a serious progress bug. I finally quit the game and go online to find out the answer (,which can be a frustrating thing to have to do for a video game). I find out that I had the correct suspect and had the correct evidence at one point in my many attempts, but the location I was attempting the arrest in was incorrect and the suspect was actually in the area where his parents live.
I was incredibly frustrated with this given that the game not only was telling me in my failed attempts that searching for the suspect in the area where his parents live fails to produce a suspect, but also that the 'correct' evidence to produce was not what your AI partner told you to provide and was not even in the top 3 pieces of evidence that seemed like the logical choice. This poor communication in the instruction, misinformation, and seemingly inflexible choice to go about the arrest made for an all-around frustrating experience in an otherwise good game (minus the aforementioned bug I came across).
Given Steam's policy of not being able to play games after 2 hours of play, I was unable to refund the game. I certainly understand having such a policy in place and I'm not blaming the developers for this complaint, but it only adds frustration when you run into so many issues in a game that inhibit progress and point to poor design and oversight after only 3 hours of play. I love the aesthetic, premise, and mechanics of Mainlining, but my frustration with the game (and Steam) has lead me not to continue playing this game.

review_text_raw:
Summary: The story was pretty good, and has other things going for it, but it feels really unpolished, poor UI, typos etc.

Things I did like: The story was engaging, and the writers did a good job in making their points about government surveillance. The core hacking gameplay is also good (albeit not very realistic but this is at least explained in game). They did a good job theming the OSes.

Things I didn't like: The UI is not good, I get that they aren't going to recode in a whole desktop environment, but you can't resize windows, text files that are opened cannot be minimized nor do they show up in the taskbar. This makes windows all overlap in an annoying way. The other thing I didn't like is the lack of continuity between cases. Changing the IP addresses each case is annoying. The fact I couldn't take more than like 256 characters of notes in the notepad app is also annoying. You can't move your cursor back to insert something into text, you have to delete it and start over.

Its weird the game's narrative and the story cases all link together but the gamestate basically wipes at each case. For example I would have liked to keep a list of websites I visited, as well as persons of interest and details about each. But because the notes are all deleted from case to case (in fact they are deleted as soon as you close the notepad app). It makes that pointless. Files are the same way, all your downloaded files are deleted from case to case. Sometimes in a detective game its useful to go back to reference old info, even if its not immediately useful for solving the case. I just felt that the game's mechanics kept holding me back from being fully immersed in the game.

There are also alot of typos. Some of which are in important places.

The way you turn in cases is also kinda clunky. Its a good idea but it ends up being frustrated on several cases. There is also not any rewards or effects on the story for getting the highest rating for cases.

This game has three elements I really like in games:

The "hacking" part, although it's very simple (hacknet, uplink etc)
The point and click game puzzle genre
an overarching story that could be interesting

So this SHOULD have been a big win for me. And yet, I had more annoyance going through the first 6 cases than fun. And that's all due to... the gameplay. 

You could ask yourself how. To summarize:
- an alternative system/desktop with some kind of mandala thing going on that'll make you dizzy if you look at it too much
- Constant chatting noises, distracting you easely from whatever path you were following. In the first few cases it's not too bad, but the BOOP BOOP BOOP continuous sound makes you mad
- Meanwhile you're trying to concentrate on the puzzles, but shit is happening at the same time, so you have to be fast. Or at least that's what the game seemingly pushes you to do. But the joy of a point and click is discovering options until you find something that clicks

It's not a hard game but the way it's build makes it unplayable, for me. I saw this comes from an old Bundlestars/Fanatical bundle that has some killer games alongside it, but this one ain't it. I'm glad I gave up, this was more stressful than working a real detective job (I'd imagine)

A cute, occasionally fun game that will often have you digging back and forth for a chain of numbers you couldn't fully memorize. With a slightly clunky U.I. and the rare bug that wouldn't let me finish a level with the correct arrest, I am a bit glad I got this on sale. Finished it with active playtime around 5 hours, and an hour of that was just realizing I had a typo and redoing a line of text. A few U.I. changes and around 5-10 more levels could make this game what it should have been.
Also, writers seem confused on tone. An adult joke jumps straight to one I'd expect from Lego City: Undercover, which is jarring.
I'd pick it up if it's under $3. Otherwise, maybe just watch a YouTuber play it out.
